scenes.title: The Bonnet Moment
scenes.setting: Master bedroom, nightstand with a lamp, mirror mounted on wall, unmade bed in soft focus
scenes.subjects: Woman, mid-30s, alone, in oversized t-shirt and joggers
scenes.action: She's wrapping a silk bonnet over freshly moisturised hair, fingers tucking edge pieces with practiced precision. Her reflection catches in the mirror as she ties the back. Small pause—a self-knowing smile. She switches off the lamp.
scenes.mood: Warm, amber lamplight. Intimate, peaceful. The softness of routine self-care. Almost meditative.
scenes.cultural_notes: The bonnet is generational wisdom—protection, intention, care ritual passed down. This is the nightly reset, the sacred hygiene moment that Black women know is non-negotiable. Speaks to hair as investment, as pride, as armor.
scenes.composition: Close-up on hands and face in mirror reflection. Soft-focus bedroom behind. Depth of field on the bonnet and her expression. Shot from slight side angle, almost documentary-observational.
scenes.products_visible: Silk bonnet (jewel-toned or patterned), leave-in conditioner bottle on nightstand, small glass of water, perhaps a hair oil in amber glass

scenes.title: Between Her Knees
scenes.setting: Living room carpet, afternoon sunlight pouring through bay window. Cushions stacked nearby.
scenes.subjects: Mother (40s, braids pulled back) and daughter (6-8 years old, in school uniform), positioned on the floor
scenes.action: Daughter sits between mother's knees, head relaxed back against her chest. Mother's hands move through her hair, fingers parting sections, weaving three-strand cornrows with rhythm. Daughter watches her fingers move in a handheld mirror. Mother hums—maybe an old song. Daughter laughs at a tickle.
scenes.mood: Golden, diffused afternoon light. Warm, unhurried, generational. The intimacy of touch and teaching. Gentle concentration.
scenes.cultural_notes: This is legacy and love made visible. The girl is learning her hair's language through her mother's hands. This scene holds centuries—the skills, the patience, the bonding. It says: we know how to care for ourselves.
scenes.composition: Wide shot from the side, capturing both figures, light streaming through the window. Low camera angle looking up at their faces. Focus on the mother's hands and the child's expression of trust and wonder.
scenes.products_visible: Hair clips, spray bottle with water, edge control in a small tub, hair butter or cream, handheld mirror, possibly coconut oil

scenes.title: Kitchen Beautician
scenes.setting: Bright kitchen, overhead natural light from window. Small table, kitchen chair, sink visible in background. Posters or plants on walls.
scenes.subjects: Two women (friends, 20s-30s, UK or US urban setting). One sitting, one standing behind with hair in her hands.
scenes.action: The standing woman is twisting the seated friend's hair into locs or installing braids. She's focused, lips slightly pressed in concentration. The seated friend is scrolling on her phone, occasionally glancing back with a grin. They're talking—catching up, laughing. A steaming mug of tea sits nearby.
scenes.mood: Daylight, pragmatic, full of laughter. This is informal, community-rooted, economical, real. No frills—just skill and friendship. Warm but energised.
scenes.cultural_notes: The kitchen beautician is embedded in Black diaspora culture—it's access, affordability, trust, and artistry all at once. This scene says: we do this for each other, in our spaces, on our time. It's entrepreneurship and sisterhood.
scenes.composition: Medium shot from the side, capturing both figures. Focus on the hands and the hair-work. The background soft and lived-in. Natural window light defining the scene.
scenes.products_visible: Hair products (oils, creams, edge control), spray bottle, bobby pins, sectioning clips, twist cream in a jar, possibly a headwrap or scarf nearby, tea mug

scenes.title: Anointing the Locs
scenes.setting: Minimalist bathroom, marble or wooden vanity, large mirror. Golden hour light flooding through a small window (morning or late afternoon).
scenes.subjects: Woman, late 20s-early 40s, shirtless or in a bralette, shoulder-length locs
scenes.action: She's standing at the mirror, unscrewing a glass jar of golden oil or shea butter. She takes a small amount between her palms, warms it by rubbing her hands together, then begins to work it through her locs methodically—from root to tip. Her eyes stay on the mirror. No rush. Pure ritual.
scenes.mood: Sensual, meditative, almost spiritual. Golden, glowing light. Peaceful. Self-reverence. The intimacy of touching your own body with intention.
scenes.cultural_notes: Locs are covenant—a visible commitment to natural texture and identity. Oiling them is a sacred act of maintenance, a moment of return to self. This speaks to the beauty-as-spirituality thread in Black women's culture.
scenes.composition: Close-up, almost portrait-like. Hands, shoulders, the locs, and her face in the mirror. Shallow depth of field. Shot slightly off-centre (rule of thirds). Golden light creating halos and texture.
scenes.products_visible: Glass jar of natural oil (argan, jojoba, or coconut oil in amber or clear glass), possibly a small wooden comb, natural or wooden hair picks, perhaps a silk scarf on the edge of the vanity

scenes.title: The Fade Moment
scenes.setting: Barbershop interior, mirror-lined walls, clippers and tools on a shelf, barber chair. Bright shop lighting, maybe neon or clean fluorescent.
scenes.subjects: Barber (any gender, 30s-50s, master of their craft) and client (young man, 18-30, getting a fresh cut)
scenes.action: The barber is running clippers up the side of the client's head, creating a sharp fade. The client's head is tilted, eyes forward but relaxed. The barber's hands are steady, confident. A moment of focus and artistry. Perhaps the barber tilts the client's head gently to catch the line just right.
scenes.mood: Focused, professional, proud. Clean, well-lit, precise. There's ritual here too—the barber as artist and keeper of standards. Masculine energy, but tender in its attention.
scenes.cultural_notes: The barbershop is a sanctuary—a place where Black men and masculine-presenting folks gather, where standards are held, where craft is visible and celebrated. The fade is identity. This scene honours skill and the spaces we've built for ourselves.
scenes.composition: Side profile of the client and barber, captured in the mirror behind the chair. Focus on the clippers and the line being cut. Slight depth of field. Professional, documentary-style framing.
scenes.products_visible: Clippers (corded or cordless), trimmer, clipper guard, aftershave or edge oil, perhaps a barber's brush, towel draped over the chair, small bottles of hair product on shelves behind

scenes.title: Dad's Saturday Hair Day
scenes.setting: Bright bedroom or living room with morning natural light streaming through window, Saturday morning energy. UK/US home with cozy, lived-in feel. Hair products, elastics, and a small stool or the edge of a bed visible.
scenes.subjects: Black father (30s-40s) and young daughter (5-7 years old). Both in comfortable weekend clothes—dad in t-shirt, daughter in a nightgown or play clothes.
scenes.action: Dad carefully sectioning his daughter's hair into sections, preparing to do her week's protective style. Daughter sitting between his knees on the floor or small stool, slightly fidgeting. Hair products—leave-in conditioner, edge control, hair oil—sit nearby in a small basket or on a nearby table. Dad's hands are focused, methodical. Maybe daughter is watching a tablet or chatting, or occasionally reaching back to touch the product bottles with curiosity.
scenes.mood: Tender, slightly uncertain but deeply committed. Warm, intimate, Saturday-morning unhurried. There's vulnerability in his concentration—he wants to get this right for her. Genuine connection over perfection. A bit of morning lightness and humor.
scenes.cultural_notes: Mirrors the mother-daughter braiding scene but centers paternal care and engagement with textured hair. Responds to cultural shift toward visible fatherhood and caregiving masculinity. Shows that hair care is not maternal-exclusive labor but family practice. Resonates with diaspora fathers reclaiming active roles in children's grooming and cultural identity maintenance.
scenes.composition: Wide shot capturing both figures with morning light as key light. Dad slightly out of focus in background, daughter's head and shoulders in focus. Or close-up of hands working through hair with daughter's patient/curious face in soft focus. Natural window light only—warm, golden, unhurried. Could be shot from side angle showing profile of concentration.
scenes.products_visible: Leave-in conditioner bottle, hair oil (amber glass dropper bottle), edge control in small jar, hair elastics in bright colors, wide-tooth comb, spray bottle for moisture.
